paper_title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents Lang Mo1,* Xingxuan Zhang1,*, Qi Wang1 Mingchao Hao1 Hao Yuan1 Chunjing Gan1 Wang Lu1 Peng Cui2, 1Stable AI *Equal contribution. 2Tsinghua University Corresponding authors. Contact: 12332894@mail.sustech.edu.cn xingxuanzhang@hotmail.com cuip@tsinghua.edu.cn ABSTRACT Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. Learning these relationships requires mechanism that turns historical evidence into predictions. We formulate agent decision making through general-purpose conditional inference, introducing Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture in which shared pretrained learner serves heterogeneous decision roles. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either models neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments thus share common evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. We instantiate the conditional predictor with LimiX-2, pretrained on structured data, which is shared across all evaluated decision roles. Across five task categories, DPDM accepts representations from semantic encoders such as Qwen3.5. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBenchs BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, the absolute gain in mean balanced accuracy is 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks. 1 Introduction generalist agent must learn how to decide, as well as understand what it is asked to do. Large language models support few-shot adaptation [2], multi-step reasoning [28], and interactive tool use [29]. The value of particular choice depends on the conditions under which it is made. Adaptive retrieval studies show that queries benefit from different retrieval strategies [9], while work on test-time computation shows that effective allocation depends on problem difficulty [22]. These findings motivate distinction between representing decision problem and learning the relationships that determine an appropriate choice. Semantic competence expands the range of problems an agent can interpret, while learning from feedback determines how effectively it can adapt its decisions to those problems. Effective learning from experience connects historical feedback to current decisions. Retrieved trajectories and reflective feedback can improve subsequent behavior [36, 21], and language models can learn numerical relationships from in-context examples [26]. The resulting decision depends on how the learner interprets the evidence. previously successful action may be inappropriate under different conditions, while frequently selected action may appear effective because of the situations in which it was used. The agent must identify conditional relationships across observations and apply them to the current decision. We distinguish two sources of decision error: information that the available history does not reveal, and information that the learning mechanism fails to use. Growing histories tests the value of additional evidence (Section 3.3), while comparing learners on identical histo01 ries tests how effectively they use that evidence (Section 3.2). This distinction separates acquiring more informative experience from improving the computation that converts existing evidence into choice. Existing approaches organize this computation in ExpeL extracts insights and redifferent ways. calls experience [34]; Rememberer updates an external experience memory using reinforcement-learning feedback [31]. Algorithm Distillation learns from reinforcement-learning histories [10], DPT predicts optimal actions from interaction contexts [11], and PreDeToR pretrains reward prediction across related decision tasks [15]. SayCan combines language planning with learned skill values [8]. These precedents establish several forms of experience-based adaptation and computational specialization. Within languagemodel-centered systems, reasoning and action generation remain closely integrated [29], and retrieved experience can be interpreted through the same language model [34]. This organization couples semantic interpretation, empirical inference, and answer generation within one pretrained mechanism. The mechanism for learning deployment-specific relationships is not exposed as separately replaceable component, limiting the ability to improve empirical inference independently of the language policy. Semantic competence alone does not establish how effectively that mechanism uses given history. The architectural choice is whether the language model should both represent decision problem and learn its deployment-specific relationships, or whether shared conditional learner should infer those relationships from historical feedback. We develop an explicit separation between semantic representation and history-conditioned prediction, making each replaceable and independently improvable component of the decision architecture. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), framework that reformulates task-defined agent decisions as conditional prediction problems. Each decision specifies its visible context, candidate descriptions, and target, while historical records provide observations of that target under related conditions. language model serves as the semantic encoder, representing the problem and candidate answers. shared conditional predictor uses the represented history to estimate the unknown target for the current decision, and decision rule converts the prediction into choice. Pretraining conditional predictor across datasets provides foundation for this construction, as established by Prior-Data Fitted Networks and Contextual Mechanism Networks [7, 33]. DPDM connects this learning capability to semantically rich agent decisions through representations of past experience and the current decision context. Tool applicability, candidate preference, and reasoning assessment become different prediction targets for the same learning mechanism. When actionoutcome observations are available, the conditional predictor can estimate consequences for objective-dependent selection. We instantiate the conditional predictor with LimiX2 [32, 33], structured-data foundation model pretrained for conditional prediction. It conditions on the available historical feedback to estimate the current target. Both neural models remain frozen as the history changes. The architecture exposes separate routes to improvement: better semantic representations can reveal relevant distinctions, and advances in conditional prediction can improve target estimates using those distinctions and historical feedback. Predictions can also support different objectives when they retain the information required by the decision rule. Across decision categories and semantic encoders, single frozen conditional predictor improves mean decision accuracy over few-shot prompting. Gains persist with identical histories and queries, showing that additional records alone do not explain the advantage. On ToolPRMBench BFCL, DPDM achieves an absolute accuracy gain of 34.26% over few-shot prompting at the methods respective evaluated history budgets. Growing-history and imbalanced-history evaluations show benefits from both accumulating experience and making better use of the same feedback. Controls demonstrate complementary contributions from historical inputtarget relationships, distinct observations, and semantic features. In separate timing study with matched histories and query sets, the equal-task mean reduction in measured full-pipeline GPU time, including historical preparation, is 80.3% relative to cached few-shot prompting. These findings support an architecture in which the mechanism for learning from experience is shared across decision roles, while each task supplies its own evidence and query without taskspecific neural-parameter updates. Learning from experience becomes an explicit target of foundation-model development. Systems such as Voyager retain accumulated experience as reusable skills [27]. DPDM develops complementary route: shared conditional predictor turns taskrelevant observations into new judgments. Improving that predictor can benefit multiple decision roles through the same interface, alongside advances in the semantic encoder that represents the problem. 2 Method Our architecture separates understanding decision problem from using historical feedback to resolve it. semantic encoder represents the current context and candidate choices, shared conditional predictor estimates the decision target from represented historical examples, and decision rule selects the answer (Figure 1). We instantiate the conditional predictor with Figure 1. DPDM uses historical feedback to make the current decision. semantic encoder represents each record, and shared conditional predictor, instantiated here with LimiX-2, estimates the current target from history. The diagram follows the main benchmark: historical targets are supplied separately from record representations, and the highest-probability candidate answer is selected. LimiX-2. Section 3.3 evaluates this adaptation by expanding historical sets and predicting the same queries. 3 Experiments We test whether shared frozen predictor supports heterogeneous decision roles and semantic encoders, whether additional history improves decisions without neural-parameter updates, and which properties of the evidence account for those gains. Across 50 benchmarks, we compare DPDM with direct prompting of the same Qwen3.5 and Llama-3.1 models, including identical-history comparisons. The last row gives the equal-task arithmetic mean. 4 Discussion and Conclusion 4.1 Discussion Learning from experience as foundation-model capability. The central implication is architectural: an agents capacity to learn from deployment experience can be developed through pretrained model dedicated to conditional prediction. Language pretraining supplies knowledge for interpreting requests, contexts, and candidate choices. Conditional pretraining supplies mechanism for learning relationships from the records available in particular deployment. Connecting these capabilities allows semantic understanding and empirical learning to contribute to the same decision. The value of the separation is that it gives learning from experience an explicit role in agent design, with its own training objectives and evaluation criteria. Relation to prior work. This proposal brings together two research directions. ExpeL extracts insights from experience and retrieves examples to guide an LLM agent [34]. DPT learns to predict optimal actions from in-context interaction data [11], while Prior-Data Fitted Networks pretrain conditional predictors across sampled prediction problems [16]. ICR-RL and BC-ICL apply general predictive foundation models to control and contextual-bandit decisions [20, 6]. DPDM connects conditional predictors to semantically expressed decision tasks through language-model representations. Each task retains its own meaning and target, while the learning mechanism operates on represented records and their labels. The use of LimiX-2 across semantic encoders illustrates how this organization can accommodate different ways of representing problem. It also creates common interface for evaluating future conditional predictors with the same semantic encoders. makes experience What valuable. The informationinference distinction clarifies how this architecture can improve. New observations can reveal relationships that the existing history leaves uncertain; improving the learner can make more effective use of relationships already supported by that history. These are different research goals. records value therefore depends on what it adds about the current decision and on the mechanism used to interpret it. The history-growth and imbalanced-history analyses give concrete examples of this principle. They motivate studying how agents collect and retain feedback alongside how conditional predictors are pretrained to learn from it. Under this view, deployment history helps determine the decision function instantiated for the current setting. 08 4.2 Conclusion We propose an architecture for agent decision making in which semantic understanding and learning from experience are distinct, connected foundation-model capabilities. By expressing task-defined decisions as conditional prediction problems, language-model representations allow shared conditional predictor to use deployment histories across heterogeneous tasks. The LimiX-2 instantiation demonstrates gains across semantic encoders, growing histories, and imbalanced feedback. This architecture provides common interface through which advances in learning from experience can improve decisions across agent tasks. URL https://arxiv.org/ abs/2610.17309. 10 Experimental Instantiation This section describes the evaluated DPDM implementation, which pairs frozen semantic encoder with LimiX-2. The lexical features, native fields, and dimensionality-reduction methods described below specify this implementation. A.1 Task Records and Historical Feedback For each task, record contains the visible input fields and candidate descriptions. The task specification defines the question to be answered and the mapping between answers and labels. For example, BFCL Callability supplies user request and function schemas; the target indicates whether any supplied function is applicable. The same specification is used for historical records and queries. Each record becomes one feature row. LimiX-2 receives the historical rows, their observed labels, and the query row whose label is to be predicted. Labels and source-group identifiers are excluded from the record features. Where source groups are defined, history and queries are separated by group. Numerical history budgets use nested prefixes of randomly permuted historical pool, sampled without replacement or class balancing. Fullpool conditions retain the original record order. Appendix gives the evaluation budgets and sampling settings. A.2 Record Representations Each record is encoded independently using its task question and candidate descriptions. Qwen and Llama use their native chat templates with text-only inputs; Qwen thinking is disabled. The feature row combines three components: Semantic features. We read the final postnormalization hidden state at the last nonpadding prompt token, before answer generation. States from multiple target prompts are concatenated, L2-normalized, and compressed by PCA to at most 32 dimensions. Lexical features. TF-IDF features [19] represent the visible text fields, with history-fitted dimensionality reduction using truncated SVD when applicable [3]. Native fields. Available numeric and categorical fields accompany the text features. Categorical mappings and numeric scaling are fitted on the historical inputs; unseen query categories are treated as missing values. Feature transformations are fitted only on historical inputs and applied unchanged to queries. As history grows, these transformations are refitted while both neural models remain frozen. Encoded states can be reused when the encoder, prompt renderer, and task specification are unchanged. The controls in Appendix specify when the fitted transformation is held fixed across conditions. A.3 From Predictions to Decisions All tasks use the same frozen LimiX-2 model with 32pipeline aggregation. Prediction uses all supplied historical rows, with retrieval disabled. LimiX-2 estimates label probabilities from these rows and the current query. For more than ten observed classes, deterministic label hierarchy combines parent and leaf probabilities to recover probabilities for the original task labels. Classes absent from history initially receive zero probability. history containing one observed class produces probability of one for that class without invoking LimiX-2. Candidates unavailable for the current query are then removed and the remaining probabilities normalized. If no probability mass remains, the valid candidates receive equal probabilities. The candidate with the highest probability is selected, with ties resolved by candidate order. The controlled outcome example supplies numeric contextaction inputs directly to LimiX-2 and selects the action with the highest predicted success probability. Benchmark Inventory The evaluation covers 50 benchmarks across five decision categories. Each benchmark defines concrete decision and its reference target. DPDM uses historical feedback to predict that target for the current input. The 82 task configurations span five categories: Agent tasks. Inputs include requests, available tools, reasoning steps, or candidate responses. Targets specify an intent, tool applicability, response type, step assessment, or preferred response. This category includes Banking77, TREC, Google Wellformed Query, BFCL Callability, ToolACE, ToolPRMBench, AgentProcess, CodeCritic, and HHRLHF. Knowledge QA. Tasks include answer selection and reasoning-step judgments from questions, passages, and candidate answers or steps. Examples include ARC, CommonsenseQA, HellaSwag, HaluEval, PRM800K, and BIG-Bench Mistake. Evidence consistency. Claims, responses, or sentence pairs are judged against their supExamples include FaithBench, plied context. RAGTruth, and natural-language inference tasks. Safety and reliability. Messages, responses, or reports are assigned task-defined risk or reliability labels. Examples include BeaverTails, ToxicChat, hate-speech datasets, ADE Corpus, and FaithDials dialogue-response hallucination judgments. 11 Language understanding. Text is assigned topic, sentiment, emotion, or linguistic label. Examples include AG News, TweetEval Sentiment, Emo, and grammatical-acceptability tasks. BFCL Callability asks whether any supplied function applies to user request [17]. The responsemode task derived from ToolACE predicts whether the next response is text, one tool call, or multiple its targets come from the response structure calls; in the source records [14]. ToolPRMBenchs BFCL, ToolSandbox, and ToolTalk suites evaluate judgments about tool-use steps [12]. Thus BFCL Callability and ToolPRMBench-BFCL have different inputs and targets. BIG-Bench Mistake supplies question, preceding reasoning, and the current step, whose correctness is the target [24]. CodeCritic includes Code and QA assessment tasks [30]. PRM800K evaluates reasoning steps [13]. The scores in this paper measure these individual labeled judgments. Each task supplies query set, separate historical pool, and target definition.
